Novo's Wegovy® was associated with a reduction in food noise according to real-world studies at ObesityWeek® 2026

Nov 14, 2026, 12:15 ET

Share this article

  • Statistically significant reductions in food noise scores from baseline were observed in adults taking semaglutide injection within the first month of initiation and through six months in the SIGNAL study1
  • Oral semaglutide was associated with about a 25% reduction from baseline in reported average food noise scores over three months in the OCTANE study. Most adults (86.4%) reported at least one treatment improvement2
  • Food noise is an emerging area of research in obesity care, with real-world studies suggesting semaglutide may provide an additional patient-centered benefit beyond weight loss1-3

PLAINSBORO, N.J. and BAGSVÆRD, Denmark, Nov. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Novo Nordisk presented real-world findings from the SIGNAL and OCTANE studies at ObesityWeek® 2026, looking at how food noise scores changed for adults with overweight or obesity taking Wegovy® injection or Wegovy® pill.1,2 Both retrospective cohort analyses used de-identified patient data from the Ro telehealth platform and a validated seven-item questionnaire to assess food noise, defined as persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts about food.3

"Patients at our center often describe persistent and intrusive thoughts about food, and that managing those thoughts can take a toll on their day-to-day lives," said Louis J. Aronne, MD, Director of the Comprehensive Weight Control Center, Weill Cornell Medicine, and co-author of the studies. "The SIGNAL and OCTANE findings showed that semaglutide injection and oral semaglutide were associated with early reductions in food noise in real-world studies. Looking forward, additional research can help clarify the clinical relevance of such food noise and its place in everyday obesity care."

The two presented studies examined changes in patient-reported food noise scores over time among adults with overweight or obesity taking semaglutide in a real-world telehealth setting, using the validated seven-item Ro Allison Indiana Dhurandhar–Food Noise Inventory (RAID-FN) questionnaire, which measures persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts about food.1,2
